chunks: And by this chain, that Abu Dajjana Al-Ansary wore a turban on the Day of Uhud with his own turban and let the tail of the turban hang between his shoulders until he began to swagger, so the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Indeed, this is a walk that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, hates, except when fighting in the way of Allah.'

key_terms.أَبُو دُجَانَةَ: Abu Dajjana, a companion of the Prophet known for his strength and stature.
key_terms.عَذَبَةَ الْعِمَامَةِ: The tail or end of the turban.
key_terms.لِمِشْيَةٌ: A manner of walking or gait.
key_terms.يَتَبَخْتَرُ: He swaggered or walked boastfully, showing off his stature or attire.
key_terms.يَوْمَ أُحُدٍ: The Day of Uhud, referring to the major battle between Muslims and Quraysh.

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the swaggering walk (takhattur) mentioned in the hadith of Abu Dajjana?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Kafi* highlights the distinction between *kibr* (arrogant pride) and legitimate confidence in the context of *Jihad*, a key theme in Shia ethical jurisprudence. It establishes that the physical manifestation of pride, such as Abu Dajjana’s swaggering gait with his turban, is divinely disliked unless it serves the purpose of inspiring troops or demonstrating strength in battle. This incident is frequently cited by scholars to illustrate the principle that actions are judged by their intent and context, particularly in the sphere of military conduct.
